lessons.title: Types of Reaction: Redox, Acids and Neutralisation
lessons.description: Oxidation, reduction, the reactivity series, acid reactions, pH scale and making salts.
lessons.content_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons. These two processes always happen simultaneously in redox reactions. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

For example, when copper oxide is reduced by carbon: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\). The copper oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced); the carbon gains oxygen (it is oxidised). The carbon is the reducing agent and copper oxide is the oxidising agent.

Key Fact

In a redox reaction, the oxidising agent causes the oxidation of another substance but is itself reduced. The reducing agent causes the reduction of another substance but is itself oxidised. This is a common source of confusion — always track both substances separately.

At Higher Tier you must also explain redox in terms of electron transfer. In the reaction between magnesium and oxygen: \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-\) (magnesium is oxidised — it loses electrons); \(O_2 + 4e^- \rightarrow 2O^{2-}\) (oxygen is reduced — it gains electrons). The substance that loses electrons is the reducing agent; the substance that gains electrons is the oxidising agent.

The Reactivity Series

The reactivity series lists metals in order of their tendency to react — specifically, how readily each metal is oxidised (loses electrons). Metals above hydrogen in the series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Metals higher in the series can displace metals lower in the series from their salt solutions — these are called displacement reactions.

The order of metals in the reactivity series can be remembered using a mnemonic. From most reactive to least reactive, the series runs: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas. Metals below hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) do not react with dilute acids. This knowledge allows chemists to predict whether a given displacement reaction is possible: if a more reactive metal is added to a salt solution of a less reactive metal, a displacement will occur. If the added metal is less reactive than the metal in solution, no reaction takes place.

When zinc is added to copper sulfate solution: \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\). Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution. Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons, forms \(Zn^{2+}\)) and copper ions are reduced (gain electrons, form Cu atoms). The blue colour of the copper sulfate solution fades as colourless zinc sulfate forms, and a reddish copper deposit appears. This is both a displacement reaction and a redox reaction.

Acids, Alkalis and the pH Scale

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH below 7 indicates an acidic solution (high concentration of \(H^+\) ions); pH 7 is neutral; above 7 is alkaline (high concentration of \(OH^-\) ions). Strong acids (such as hydrochloric acid, HCl) fully dissociate in water into ions, whereas weak acids (such as ethanoic acid) only partially dissociate. It is important to distinguish between a strong acid (degree of ionisation) and a concentrated acid (amount of acid dissolved per litre) — a concentrated weak acid is not the same as a strong acid.

Key Fact

Strong acid: fully dissociates into ions in water (e.g. HCl \(\rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-\)). Weak acid: partially dissociates (e.g. ethanoic acid). Concentrated: many moles of acid per litre. Dilute: few moles per litre. These are independent properties — a strong acid can be dilute.

Neutralisation and Making Salts

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base or alkali. The general equation is: acid + base → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide: \(HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\). At the ionic level, the \(H^+\) ion from the acid reacts with the \(OH^-\) ion from the alkali: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Acids also react with metals, carbonates and metal oxides. Key reactions to know:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (e.g. \(Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2\))
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (e.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\))
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water (e.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\))

In your practical work (PAG C2), you will carry out acid-alkali titrations to find the volume of acid needed to exactly neutralise a given volume of alkali. A suitable indicator (e.g. methyl orange or phenolphthalein) is added to the alkali in a conical flask. Acid is added from a burette drop by drop until the indicator changes colour permanently at the end point. The titration is repeated without indicator to produce a pure salt solution, which can be evaporated carefully to obtain crystals. Concordant results (within 0.10 cm3 of each other) are used to calculate the mean titre.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common error in 3-mark Explain questions on redox is confusing the oxidising agent with the substance that gets oxidised. Remember: the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced (it oxidises something else). For questions on acids, do not use ‘strong’ and ‘concentrated’ interchangeably — examiners penalise this substitution. In salt-preparation questions, name the acid correctly: HCl makes chloride salts, H2SO4 makes sulfate salts, HNO3 makes nitrate salts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of electrons. OIL RIG is the key mnemonic. The oxidising agent is itself reduced; the reducing agent is itself oxidised.
  • The reactivity series orders metals by reactivity. More reactive metals displace less reactive metals from salt solutions — these are redox reactions. Strong acids fully dissociate in water; weak acids partially dissociate. ‘Strong’ and ‘concentrated’ are not synonyms.
  • Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Key reactions: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO2; acid + metal oxide → salt + water. The salt formed depends on the acid used.

lessons.title: Electrolysis of Molten and Aqueous Compounds
lessons.description: Why electrolysis works, electrode reactions, electrolysis of brine, and aluminium extraction.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to decompose an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte, and it must be either molten or dissolved in water so that the ions are free to move and carry charge.

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes: the cathode (negative electrode) and the anode (positive electrode). Positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode; negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode. A useful mnemonic is PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Key Fact

At the cathode (negative): positive ions gain electrons — this is reduction. At the anode (positive): negative ions lose electrons — this is oxidation. Remember: electrolysis involves both oxidation and reduction simultaneously.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

When a molten ionic compound is electrolysed, only the ions of that compound are present. The metal ion moves to the cathode and is deposited as the metal; the non-metal ion moves to the anode and is released as the non-metal element. For example, molten lead bromide produces lead metal at the cathode and bromine gas at the anode. The key requirement is that the compound is molten — solid ionic compounds cannot conduct electricity because the ions are held in a fixed lattice and are not free to move. Dissolving the compound in water also frees the ions, though this introduces additional complexity because water provides its own ions.

It is important to understand that the electrolyte is not simply “broken down” into smaller pieces — it is chemically decomposed into its constituent elements. This makes electrolysis a powerful tool for extracting reactive metals that cannot be produced by simpler reduction methods. The external electrical supply acts as an electron pump: the power supply removes electrons from the anode (making it positive) and pushes electrons into the cathode (making it negative). Ions in the electrolyte carry charge through the solution between the electrodes, completing the circuit.

For molten lead bromide electrolysis:

Cathode (reduction): \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\)

Anode (oxidation): \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\)

Half-equations must be balanced for both atoms and charge. At the cathode, electrons are gained (shown on the left side of the arrow). At the anode, electrons are released (shown on the right side). The number of electrons must cancel when the two half-equations are combined.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the solution also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water itself. This means there is competition at each electrode between different ions. The rules for predicting products are:

  • Cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced from \(H^+\) ions. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.
  • Anode: If a halide ion (Cl23, Br23, I23) is present in large amounts, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions).

Brine is concentrated sodium chloride solution. During electrolysis of brine, three useful products are obtained:

  • Cathode: hydrogen gas is produced (sodium is too reactive to be deposited; \(H^+\) ions are discharged instead).
  • Anode: chlorine gas is produced (chloride ions are present in high concentration and are preferentially discharged).
  • Remaining solution: sodium hydroxide (NaOH) remains in solution, as the sodium and hydroxide ions are not discharged.

The three products — hydrogen, chlorine, and sodium hydroxide — are all industrially important: chlorine is used to make bleach and PVC; hydrogen is used as a fuel; sodium hydroxide is used to make soap and paper.

Extraction of Aluminium

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon. Instead, it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)). The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and reduce energy costs.

Key Fact

Aluminium is deposited at the cathode (\(Al^{3+}\) ions gain electrons). Oxygen is released at the anode (\(O^{2-}\) ions lose electrons). The carbon anodes gradually burn away because the oxygen produced reacts with them at high temperature, so they need regular replacement. The process uses large amounts of electricity, making aluminium expensive to produce.

Practical Electrolysis (PAG C2)

In your practical work (PAG C2), you will investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert (carbon) electrodes. A typical investigation uses copper sulfate solution or brine. To test the gases produced: hold a lit splint near the cathode to detect hydrogen (squeaky pop); hold damp litmus paper near the anode to detect chlorine (paper bleaches) or use a glowing splint to detect oxygen (relights). Record which gas appears at which electrode and compare your results with predictions from competition rules.

Electroplating is another important application of electrolysis. To electroplate an object with copper: make the object the cathode, use a copper electrode as the anode, and use copper sulfate solution as the electrolyte. Copper atoms at the anode dissolve into solution as copper ions; the same mass of copper deposits on the cathode. The object gains a thin, evenly spread copper layer. Electroplating is used in jewellery (silver plating), corrosion protection (zinc plating on steel, called galvanising) and in electronics (copper tracks on circuit boards).

Higher Tier half-equations for aluminium extraction:

Cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\)

Anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\)
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions on electrolysis of aqueous solutions, always check whether the metal is more or less reactive than hydrogen — this determines whether you get hydrogen gas or the metal at the cathode. At the anode, halide ions take priority over hydroxide ions (so chlorine is produced from brine, not oxygen). A very common error is stating that sodium is produced at the cathode during electrolysis of brine — sodium is too reactive, so hydrogen is produced instead. Higher Tier: when writing half-equations, always balance atoms first, then balance charge using electrons. State clearly which electrode each half-equation applies to.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis uses electricity to decompose ionic compounds. The electrolyte must be molten or dissolved. Positive ions move to the cathode (reduction — gain electrons); negative ions move to the anode (oxidation — lose electrons). PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
  • In aqueous solutions, competition occurs between ions. Cathode: hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; metal is deposited if less reactive. Anode: halide ions → halogen produced; no halide → oxygen produced. Electrolysis of brine gives hydrogen (cathode), chlorine (anode), and sodium hydroxide (remaining solution).
  • Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite (to lower the melting point). Aluminium forms at the cathode; oxygen at the anode. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing. The process is energy-intensive and therefore expensive.

lessons.title: Identifying Substances: Flame Tests and Gas Tests
lessons.description: Flame tests for metal ions, tests for gases, precipitate tests and instrumental analysis.
lessons.content_html:
Why We Need Chemical Tests

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances — whether to check the safety of a water supply, verify the purity of a product, identify minerals in rocks, or analyse a sample in a forensic investigation. Chemical identification tests — collectively known as qualitative analysis — fall into two broad categories: traditional wet chemistry tests that rely on observable changes, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more precise results.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Electrons in the metal ion absorb energy from the flame, are promoted to a higher energy level, and then release that energy as visible light at a characteristic wavelength. To carry out a flame test: clean a nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove residues from previous tests), dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The loop must be cleaned between each test to avoid contamination that could give a misleading result.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green or blue-green. Barium — apple-green.

Tests for Gases

You must be able to test for four common gases. Each test gives a distinctive, reproducible result:

  • Hydrogen — hold a lit splint near the mouth of the tube; a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen (it ignites and reacts with oxygen in the air).
  • Oxygen — insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion.
  • Carbon dioxide — bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); it turns milky (white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms): \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\).
  • Chlorine — hold damp litmus paper near the gas; it is first turned red (chlorine is acidic) then bleached white (chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent).

Testing for Metal Ions with Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to a solution containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The metal ions react with hydroxide ions to form insoluble metal hydroxides, whose colour identifies the ion present.

Calcium (Ca2+): white precipitate. Copper(II) (Cu2+): blue precipitate. Iron(II) (Fe2+): green precipitate (\(Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\)). Iron(III) (Fe3+): brown precipitate (\(Fe^{3+} + 3OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\)). Aluminium (Al3+): white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric). Magnesium (Mg2+): white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This distinction between aluminium and magnesium — both give white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves — is frequently tested.

Testing for Negative Ions (Anions)

Carbonate ions (CO32-): add dilute hydrochloric acid; if carbonates are present, carbon dioxide is produced (test it by bubbling through limewater — it turns milky). Sulfate ions (SO42-): acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid first (to remove interfering ions), then add barium chloride solution; a white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfates. Halide ions: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions give a white precipitate of silver chloride; bromide ions give a cream precipitate; iodide ions give a yellow precipitate.

Key Fact

Halide identification: add silver nitrate (after acidifying with dilute nitric acid). Chloride → white precipitate. Bromide → cream precipitate. Iodide → yellow precipitate. Always acidify first to remove carbonate or other interfering ions.

Systematic Approach to Identifying an Unknown Ionic Compound

When identifying an unknown ionic compound, work through the tests in a logical order. Begin by dissolving a small amount of the sample in distilled water. Carry out a flame test to identify the metal cation: note the colour carefully and compare against the reference list. If the flame test result is ambiguous (for example, a sodium impurity masking potassium), confirm using a sodium hydroxide precipitate test. Next, test for the anion: use dilute acid and limewater for carbonates, barium chloride solution for sulfates, and acidified silver nitrate for halides. Record all observations clearly — both positive (what you see) and negative (what is absent). Always repeat tests if an observation is unclear, and clean equipment between each test to avoid contamination.

Instrumental Methods and Flame Emission Spectroscopy (Higher Tier)

Instrumental methods such as gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (often combined as GC-MS) are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional wet chemistry tests. They can detect very small quantities of a substance and give quantitative results rather than just qualitative observations.

Flame emission spectroscopy passes the light from a flame test through a prism or diffraction grating to produce a spectrum of the light emitted by each element. Each element produces a unique set of coloured lines at specific wavelengths. Unlike a visual flame test, this technique can: detect very small quantities of metal ions, identify ions even when a mixture of metals is present (the spectrum shows lines for each), and give quantitative information about concentration (by measuring line intensity). A simple flame test only gives a single colour that may mask one ion when another is present (e.g. sodium’s intense yellow can mask potassium’s lilac).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For flame test and precipitate questions, you must state both the reagent used and the observation. Writing ‘add NaOH’ without stating the colour of the precipitate will not score the second mark. For gas tests, name both the test substance and the result (e.g. ‘glowing splint relights’ for oxygen — do not just write ‘splint test’). A common error is confusing the aluminium and magnesium precipitate tests — remember only aluminium’s white precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH. Higher Tier: in questions comparing flame tests with flame emission spectroscopy, focus on the advantages of the instrumental method: can detect mixtures, gives quantitative data, much higher sensitivity.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame test colours: lithium = crimson, sodium = yellow, potassium = lilac, calcium = orange-red, copper = green, barium = apple-green. Gas tests: hydrogen = squeaky pop; oxygen = relights glowing splint; CO2 = turns limewater milky; chlorine = bleaches damp litmus paper.

lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
lessons.description: Collision theory, factors affecting reaction rate, and practical methods for measuring rate.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how quickly a reaction happens. A fast reaction, such as an explosion, is over in a fraction of a second. A slow reaction, such as the rusting of iron or the weathering of stone, takes months or years. In industry, controlling the rate of a reaction is vital — too fast can be dangerous, too slow is uneconomical.

Rate can be measured in several ways: the volume of gas produced per unit time (using a gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water), the mass of a reaction mixture lost per unit time (as gas escapes, measured using a balance), or the time taken for a colour change or for a solution to become opaque. The choice depends on the particular reaction and what can be conveniently measured.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must: (1) collide with each other, (2) collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy), and (3) collide with the correct orientation. Not every collision leads to a reaction — most are unsuccessful because the particles bounce off without reacting. The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions: collisions that have both enough energy and the right orientation.

Key Fact

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Anything that increases the frequency or energy of successful collisions increases the rate of reaction.

Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction

Four main factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction: temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts.

Temperature: Increasing the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. More importantly, a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy, so a much larger fraction of collisions are successful. Even a small increase in temperature produces a significant increase in rate.

Concentration (for solutions) and pressure (for gases): Increasing concentration means more particles in the same volume, so they collide more frequently. For gases, increasing pressure pushes particles closer together, with the same effect. More collisions per unit time → more successful collisions → faster rate.

Surface area: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio. A greater surface area means more of the solid is exposed to the other reactant, so collisions occur more frequently. Powdered marble chips react faster with hydrochloric acid than large lumps, even with the same total mass. In extreme cases, a fine powder of combustible material in air can cause a dust explosion.

Catalysts

A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. On a reaction profile, the catalyst lowers the peak (activation energy) without changing the energy levels of the reactants or products. Each catalyst is specific to a particular reaction — iron catalyses the Haber process but would not catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (which uses manganese dioxide).

Key Fact

Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up and are not changed at the end of the reaction. Enzymes are biological catalysts found in all living organisms.

Interpreting Rate of Reaction Graphs

Rate graphs typically plot volume of gas (or mass lost) on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The gradient (steepness) of the line at any point shows the rate at that moment — a steeper gradient means a faster rate. The line levels off when one reactant is used up (the reaction is complete). Two curves on the same axes that level off at the same point but with different steepnesses represent the same reaction with the same amount of reactant, but at different rates (e.g. different temperatures or concentrations).

In your practical work (PAG C5), you investigate the rate of reaction between a metal (such as magnesium) and dilute acid, or between marble chips and hydrochloric acid. Methods include:

  • Gas syringe: collect gas in a syringe and record volume at regular intervals.
  • Displacement of water: collect gas over water in an inverted measuring cylinder.
  • Mass loss: place the flask on a balance; record mass at regular intervals as gas escapes through cotton wool.
  • Disappearing cross: for the sodium thiosulfate and acid reaction, time how long it takes for a cross viewed through the solution to disappear as a precipitate of sulfur forms.

In all methods, change only one variable at a time and keep all other conditions constant to make it a fair test. Look for anomalous results in your data and exclude them when calculating means.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark Explain questions about factors affecting rate, always give a three-step answer: (1) state what changes (e.g. temperature increases), (2) link to collision theory (e.g. particles have more kinetic energy, collide more frequently and with more energy), (3) give the consequence for rate (e.g. more successful collisions per second, so rate increases). Generic responses like ‘particles collide more’ without explaining why collisions increase will only score 1 or 2 marks. A common mistake is saying catalysts are ‘used up’ — they are not, and stating this will lose marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Collision theory: particles must collide with enough energy (activation energy) and correct orientation for a reaction to occur.
  • Increasing temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases) and surface area all increase the rate by increasing the frequency and/or energy of successful collisions. Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway — they are not used up.
  • Rate graphs: steeper gradient = faster rate; the line levels off when a reactant is used up. PAG C5 involves measuring rate by gas collection (syringe or displacement) or mass loss. Change only one variable at a time for a fair test.

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Le Chatelier's Principle
lessons.description: Dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle and applying it to the Haber process conditions.
lessons.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions go to completion — the reactants are used up and only products remain. However, some reactions are reversible. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to re-form the original reactants. This is shown using the equilibrium symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) instead of a single arrow.

A well-known example is the dehydration of hydrated copper sulfate: blue hydrated copper sulfate (\(CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O\)) loses water when heated to form white anhydrous copper sulfate (\(CuSO_4\)). Adding water to the white powder restores the blue colour. Another example is the decomposition of ammonium chloride: \(NH_4Cl(s) \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + HCl(g)\). When heated, it decomposes into gases; when cooled, the gases recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by the same amount of energy. The two energy changes are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

Reversible reactions are significant in many biological and industrial contexts. The reaction between haemoglobin and oxygen in the blood is reversible: at the lungs, where oxygen concentration is high, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin; at the tissues, where oxygen concentration is low, the reverse reaction releases oxygen to the cells. This is a natural example of Le Chatelier’s principle operating in a biological system — the equilibrium position shifts depending on the local conditions. Understanding reversibility is essential for designing efficient chemical manufacturing processes, because it helps chemists choose conditions that maximise the yield of the desired product while minimising energy use and waste.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is eventually reached. At equilibrium:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal to each other).
  • Both reactions are still occurring at the molecular level — this is why the equilibrium is described as “dynamic.”

Equilibrium does not mean the amounts of reactants and products are equal — it means they are constant. The equilibrium position can strongly favour the products or the reactants. Equilibrium is not a static state — both forward and reverse reactions continue, but at equal rates, so the net composition does not change. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system; if products escape, the reaction continues in the forward direction until completion.

The position of equilibrium — how far the reaction proceeds towards products — is described qualitatively. We say the equilibrium “lies to the right” if products predominate, or “lies to the left” if reactants predominate. In many industrial reactions, chemists deliberately choose conditions that push the equilibrium position as far to the right as possible while keeping the rate acceptable. This involves an understanding of both kinetics (rate) and thermodynamics (equilibrium) working together, which is why industrial chemistry is a careful balancing act between speed and yield.

Le Chatelier’s Principle (Higher Tier)

Le Chatelier’s principle states that if the conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium position shifts in the direction that opposes the change. This allows us to predict how temperature, concentration, and pressure affect the yield of a reaction.

Temperature: Increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction (to absorb the extra heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction. This changes the yield of the reaction.

Concentration: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products (to use up the extra reactant). Increasing the concentration of a product shifts it towards the reactants. Removing a product also shifts equilibrium to the right (towards products).

Pressure (reactions involving gases): Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas (to reduce the pressure). Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas. Count the total moles of gas on each side to predict the direction of shift.

Catalyst: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position — it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the final proportions of reactants and products are unchanged. This is a frequently tested distinction.

The Haber Process: A Le Chatelier’s Example

The Haber process is the most important industrial application of Le Chatelier’s principle. It produces ammonia, which is essential for making fertilisers, explosives and cleaning products:

$$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

The forward reaction is exothermic and there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right. Applying Le Chatelier’s principle: a lower temperature favours the exothermic direction (more ammonia), but the rate would be unacceptably slow. A higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (the products), increasing yield, but very high pressures are dangerous and expensive to maintain.

Key Fact

Industrial conditions are a compromise: approximately 450°C (high enough for acceptable rate, low enough for reasonable yield), approximately 200 atm (high yield without excessive cost and safety risks), and an iron catalyst (increases rate without changing yield). Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the reactor to maximise efficiency.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions on equilibrium, always be precise: ‘the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant’ is correct; ‘the concentrations are equal’ is wrong. For Le Chatelier’s principle questions, work through the logic step by step: identify what has changed → state which direction the equilibrium shifts → explain why using Le Chatelier’s principle. A very common error is stating that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position — it does not; it only speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached. Higher Tier: in Haber process questions, always explain that the industrial conditions are a compromise between yield and rate, and cost and safety — not the theoretically optimal conditions for yield alone.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions can proceed in both directions. In a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is reached when the rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal and concentrations of reactants and products are constant (not necessarily equal). Both reactions still occur at the molecular level.
  • Higher: Le Chatelier’s principle — if conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium towards products. Catalysts do not change the equilibrium position.
  • The Haber process (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3) uses conditions of approximately 450°C, 200 atm, and an iron catalyst — a compromise between yield, rate, cost and safety. Unreacted gases are recycled.

lessons.title: Improving Processes: Metals, LCAs and Recycling
lessons.description: Metal extraction by displacement and biological methods, life cycle assessments, and recycling.
lessons.content_html:
Atom Economy and Percentage Yield

In industrial chemistry, two key measures tell us how efficiently a reaction uses its raw materials. Atom economy tells you what fraction of the mass of the reactants ends up as the wanted product rather than waste. A high atom economy means less waste is generated, lowering environmental impact and production costs.

The formula is:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield compares the actual amount of product made to the theoretical maximum:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield is often below 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, reversible reactions that do not go to completion, or product lost during purification. The limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield — once it runs out, the reaction stops regardless of how much of the other reactant remains.

Key Fact

Atom economy measures what proportion of reactant atoms become the desired product (from the balanced equation). Percentage yield measures how much product was actually made compared to the theoretical maximum. Both should be as high as possible for economic and environmental reasons.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life. The four main stages are: (1) extracting and processing raw materials, (2) manufacturing, (3) using the product (including transport and packaging), and (4) disposing of the product at the end of its useful life.

LCAs consider: energy consumption at each stage, raw material use, water use, emissions to air and water (including greenhouse gases and toxic substances), waste produced, and the potential for recycling or reuse at the end of life. However, some factors — such as visual impact, noise, or local ecosystem disruption — are difficult to quantify precisely. This means LCAs involve some subjective judgement, and different analysts can reach different conclusions if they weight factors differently. Companies sometimes use selective LCA data to support marketing claims, so evaluating LCA evidence critically is important.

Recycling

Recycling reduces the need to extract new raw materials, saves energy, and reduces the volume of waste going to landfill. Factors that affect decisions about recycling include: the cost of collection and sorting, the energy needed to process recycled material compared to making new material, the market value of the recycled product, and public willingness to separate and recycle materials.

Metals are particularly worth recycling because mining and refining metal ores is very energy-intensive. Recycling aluminium, for example, uses only a small fraction of the energy required to extract aluminium from its ore (bauxite) by electrolysis. Glass and paper can also be recycled effectively, though the economic viability depends on collection costs, sorting complexity and market conditions.

Key Fact

Recycling conserves finite resources, reduces energy use, and cuts landfill waste. Metals such as aluminium are especially valuable to recycle because extracting them from ore by electrolysis is very energy-intensive. The overall benefit must weigh the energy and cost of collection and processing.

Extracting Metals from Low-Grade Ores

Traditional smelting requires high concentrations of metal ore and generates significant environmental impact. Where ore is too dilute (low-grade) to make smelting economically viable, alternative biological methods can be used. Two techniques are particularly important: phytomining and bioleaching.

Phytomining uses plants that can absorb and accumulate metal ions from the soil through their root systems. These plants, sometimes called hyperaccumulators, concentrate metal ions in their leaves and stems. The plants are then harvested and burned; the resulting ash contains a much higher concentration of the metal compound than the original soil. The metal is then extracted from the ash, often by smelting or chemical treatment. The process is slow (growing the plants takes time) but has a lower environmental impact than traditional opencast mining.

Bioleaching uses bacteria that produce acidic solutions (leachate) by reacting with metal sulfide ores. The leachate dissolves the metal compounds out of the ore. The resulting metal-rich solution (often called the ‘pregnant leach solution’) can then have the metal extracted from it either by displacement (adding a more reactive metal) or by electrolysis. Bioleaching is also slower than conventional extraction but requires less energy input and can process waste heaps and low-grade ores that would otherwise be uneconomical to use.

Key Fact

Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal ions; the plants are burned and the metal extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metals from low-grade ores; the metal is then removed by displacement or electrolysis. Both are slower but more sustainable alternatives to conventional smelting for low-grade ores.

Traditional reduction with carbon is used for metals below carbon in the reactivity series (such as iron, zinc and copper). Carbon displaces the metal from its oxide when heated at high temperatures. Electrolysis is required for metals above carbon in the reactivity series (such as aluminium) because they cannot be displaced by carbon. Electrolysis uses large amounts of electrical energy, making it expensive. By contrast, phytomining and bioleaching require very little energy but are slow, making them best suited to low-grade or dilute ore bodies where faster methods are not viable.

Sustainability in Chemistry

The principles of sustainable chemistry combine all the ideas above: maximising atom economy to reduce waste, conducting LCAs to guide product design, recycling where possible to conserve finite resources, and using biological or lower-energy extraction methods where appropriate. Chemistry plays a central role in meeting the needs of the present without depleting resources that future generations will need.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark extended-response questions comparing extraction methods or evaluating LCAs, make sure you give both advantages and disadvantages for each method. ‘Evaluate’ means you must weigh up the evidence and reach a conclusion. For calculation questions involving atom economy or percentage yield, always show the formula, substitution and units. A common error is confusing these two measures — remember: atom economy comes from the balanced equation alone; percentage yield requires actual and theoretical values from the experiment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant mass that becomes the desired product; percentage yield measures how much of the theoretical maximum was actually obtained. Both should be maximised in green chemistry.
  • Life cycle assessments evaluate the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction through to disposal. They are partly subjective and must be interpreted critically.
  • Phytomining (using plants) and bioleaching (using bacteria) are sustainable alternatives to conventional smelting for low-grade copper ores, requiring less energy but more time.

lessons.title: Organic Chemistry: Hydrocarbons, Alcohols and Polymers
lessons.description: Crude oil fractions, alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids, and addition vs condensation polymers.
lessons.content_html:
Crude Oil and Fractional Distillation

Crude oil is a finite resource and a vital feedstock for the petrochemical industry. It is a mixture of hundreds of different hydrocarbons — molecules made up of only hydrogen and carbon atoms. The most common hydrocarbons in crude oil are alkanes.

Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation. The oil is heated so that most of it vaporises. The vapours rise up a tall fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top. Different fractions condense at different heights depending on the boiling points of their molecules. Shorter-chain molecules have weaker forces between them and lower boiling points, so they condense near the top; longer-chain molecules with stronger forces between them condense near the bottom. The main fractions include refinery gases, petrol (gasoline), kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.

Key Fact

Shorter-chain hydrocarbons have lower boiling points, lower viscosity and are more flammable. They are collected near the top of the fractionating column. Longer-chain hydrocarbons condense near the bottom, are more viscous and less easily ignited.

Alkanes

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — they have only single bonds between carbon atoms. Their general formula is \(C_nH_{2n+2}\). The first four members are methane (\(CH_4\)), ethane (\(C_2H_6\)), propane (\(C_3H_8\)) and butane (\(C_4H_{10}\)). A common exam error is writing the formula as C\(_n\)+H\(_{2n+2}\) with a plus sign — it is \(C_nH_{2n+2}\) with the subscripts joined directly.

Alkanes burn in oxygen. Complete combustion (with excess oxygen) produces carbon dioxide and water:

$$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) alongside water. Carbon monoxide is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin and prevents oxygen transport.

Cracking

There is greater demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons (for fuels and as chemical feedstocks) than for longer-chain ones. Cracking converts surplus long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful molecules. Two methods are used: catalytic cracking (passing hydrocarbon vapour over a hot catalyst at moderate temperatures) and steam cracking (mixing with steam at very high temperatures). Both methods always produce a mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes. For example:

$$C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_2H_4$$

The alkene produced (here ethene, \(C_2H_4\)) is a key raw material for making polymers. You can distinguish alkenes from alkanes using bromine water: alkenes decolourise orange bromine water to colourless (the bromine adds across the double bond), whereas alkanes produce no colour change because they are saturated.

Alkenes have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n}\) and contain at least one \(C{=}C\) double bond. Because the double bond is a site of high electron density, alkenes undergo addition reactions: molecules like hydrogen, water or bromine add across the double bond, breaking it and forming a single-bonded product. This is why alkenes are far more reactive than alkanes and are used as starting materials in chemical synthesis.

Alcohols

Alcohols are organic compounds that contain a hydroxyl functional group (–OH). The first four are methanol (\(CH_3OH\)), ethanol (\(C_2H_5OH\)), propanol (\(C_3H_7OH\)) and butanol (\(C_4H_9OH\)). Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks and is also used as a fuel and solvent.

Ethanol can be produced in two ways. Fermentation uses yeast to convert glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide under anaerobic (no oxygen) conditions at around 25–35 °C — above 40 °C the yeast enzymes denature; below ~15 °C the reaction is too slow. Hydration of ethene (a reversible reaction requiring steam and a catalyst) is a faster industrial method used when ethene is available from cracking. Fermentation uses a renewable starting material (plant sugars) whereas hydration uses a finite resource (crude oil-derived ethene).

Key Fact

Fermentation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, using yeast under anaerobic conditions at approximately 25–35 °C. Too hot and the yeast enzymes denature; too cold and the rate is unacceptably slow. The ethanol produced can be used as a biofuel or purified for drinks.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH functional group. The simplest examples are methanoic acid (\(HCOOH\)) and ethanoic acid (\(CH_3COOH\), the acid in vinegar). Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to form weakly acidic solutions. They react with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide — for example, ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate produces sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide. They also react with alcohols (in the presence of an acid catalyst) to form esters and water.

Addition polymers are made when many small alkene monomer molecules join together by opening their \(C{=}C\) double bonds. No other product is formed — all atoms end up in the polymer chain. The reaction has 100% atom economy. Common addition polymers include poly(ethene) made from ethene, and poly(propene) made from propene. The repeat unit of the polymer has the same number of carbon and hydrogen atoms as the monomer, but no double bond.

Addition polymers are widely used in packaging, containers, pipes and clothing fibres. However, they are generally non-biodegradable and can persist in the environment for a very long time, creating significant waste management challenges.

Condensation polymers are formed when two different types of monomer join together and a small molecule — usually water — is eliminated at each bond. Unlike addition polymerisation, the atom economy is less than 100% because water is lost. Examples include nylon (a polyamide, formed from diamines and dicarboxylic acids) and polyester (formed from diols and dicarboxylic acids). These materials are used in textiles, bottles and ropes. Because the monomers have two functional groups each (one at each end of the molecule), very long chains form.

Key Fact

Addition polymerisation: alkene monomers join with no other products (100% atom economy). Condensation polymerisation: monomers with two functional groups join, releasing water each time (atom economy below 100%). Examples: poly(ethene) is addition; nylon and polyester are condensation polymers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error with alkane formulae is writing the general formula with a + sign between C and H (e.g. C\(_n\)+H\(_{2n+2}\) — this is wrong). Write \(C_nH_{2n+2}\) as a continuous formula. For polymer questions, make sure you can draw the repeat unit and say whether the process is addition or condensation — the key test is whether a small molecule is eliminated. For fermentation questions, always state the conditions: anaerobic, yeast, and a temperature of approximately 25–35 °C.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation; longer chains condense lower in the column and have higher boiling points. Cracking converts long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes.
  • Alcohols contain an –OH group and can be made by fermentation (anaerobic, yeast, ~30 °C) or hydration of ethene. Carboxylic acids contain a –COOH group and are weak acids.
  • Addition polymers are formed from alkene monomers with no other products. Condensation polymers form when monomers with two functional groups join and eliminate water at each bond.

lessons.title: Earth's Atmosphere and Climate Change
lessons.description: How the atmosphere evolved, the greenhouse effect, climate change evidence, and atmospheric pollutants.
lessons.content_html:
The Current Atmosphere

The Earth’s atmosphere today is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and around 1% other gases, primarily argon, with carbon dioxide at approximately 0.04% and small amounts of water vapour. This composition has been relatively stable for around 200 million years. However, human activities are now causing measurable increases in the concentrations of certain gases — particularly carbon dioxide and methane — with significant consequences for the global climate.

How the Atmosphere Evolved

Earth’s atmosphere has changed dramatically over its approximately 4.6-billion-year history. Scientists believe the early atmosphere was produced by intense volcanic activity during the first billion years. The early atmosphere consisted mainly of carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen, along with water vapour and small amounts of methane and ammonia — resembling the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today. As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans, and much of the carbon dioxide dissolved in this new ocean water.

Around 2.7 billion years ago, early photosynthetic organisms — including algae and cyanobacteria — evolved in the oceans. Photosynthesis absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Over hundreds of millions of years, this process gradually increased oxygen levels and decreased carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere. As oxygen accumulated, it formed the ozone layer (\(O_3\)) in the upper atmosphere, which blocked harmful ultraviolet radiation and allowed life to colonise land. Some carbon dioxide also dissolved in the oceans, was incorporated into the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, and was eventually locked away in sedimentary rocks (limestone) and, over geological time, in fossil fuels.

Key Fact

The early atmosphere was mainly \(CO_2\) from volcanic activity. Photosynthesis by early organisms gradually increased oxygen and decreased carbon dioxide over billions of years. Carbon dioxide was also removed by dissolving in the oceans and becoming locked in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.

The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough to support life. Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The warm surface then emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation back towards space. Greenhouse gases — principally carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour — absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth’s surface. This traps heat energy in the lower atmosphere.

Without any greenhouse effect, the average surface temperature of Earth would be far below freezing. The problem arises when human activities increase the concentration of greenhouse gases beyond natural levels, intensifying the warming effect.

Key Fact

The three main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), methane (\(CH_4\)) and water vapour. They absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth’s surface and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards Earth, warming the lower atmosphere.

Climate Change

Human activities are increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, enhancing the natural greenhouse effect. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide that was locked away millions of years ago. Deforestation reduces the number of trees absorbing \(CO_2\) through photosynthesis. Agriculture — particularly cattle farming and flooded rice paddies — produces methane. Landfill sites release methane as organic waste decomposes anaerobically. These processes together are enhancing the greenhouse effect, causing global warming and the broader pattern of climate change.

There is a strong correlation between the rise in fossil fuel use, increasing atmospheric \(CO_2\) concentrations, and rising global average temperatures. Ice core data shows that \(CO_2\) levels today are higher than at any point over hundreds of thousands of years of ice-core records, and the current rate of increase is faster than at any previous recorded time. However, climate models are complex and depend on many interacting variables. Natural climate variations also occur — volcanic eruptions can cause temporary cooling, and solar output varies over long cycles. Despite these uncertainties, the scientific consensus is that human activities are the dominant cause of the warming trend observed since the mid-20th century.

Atmospheric Pollutants

Burning fossil fuels produces not only carbon dioxide but also several directly harmful pollutants. You need to know the source, identity and effects of each.

Carbon monoxide (CO) — produced by incomplete combustion when oxygen supply is insufficient. It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, preventing blood from carrying oxygen. High concentrations are fatal; lower concentrations cause headaches and dizziness.

Sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)) — formed when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. Reacts with water in the atmosphere to form sulfurous and sulfuric acid, falling as acid rain. Acid rain corrodes limestone buildings, damages tree foliage and acidifies lakes and rivers, harming aquatic life.

Oxides of nitrogen (\(NO_x\)) — formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the high temperatures inside vehicle engines and industrial furnaces. Also contribute to acid rain and to the formation of smog in urban areas.

Particulates (fine soot particles and other solid fragments from incomplete combustion) — can penetrate deep into the lungs, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. They also reduce visibility and can influence global temperatures by scattering or absorbing sunlight.

Key Fact

Key pollutants from burning fossil fuels: CO (incomplete combustion, toxic to blood), \(SO_2\) (sulfur in fuels, causes acid rain), \(NO_x\) (high-temperature reactions in engines, acid rain + smog), particulates (incomplete combustion, respiratory disease).

Mitigating Pollution and Climate Change

Pollution from combustion can be reduced by using catalytic converters in vehicles (which convert CO and \(NO_x\) into less harmful \(CO_2\) and \(N_2\)), removing sulfur from fuels before burning, and using flue gas desulfurisation at power stations (reacting \(SO_2\) in waste gases with calcium oxide to produce calcium sulfate). Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources, improving energy efficiency, protecting and restoring forests, and — at the individual level — reducing energy consumption and modifying diets and travel choices.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on climate change, make sure you evaluate the evidence: acknowledge the strong evidence (correlation between \(CO_2\) and temperature, ice core data) and the uncertainties (complex models, natural variation). A balanced, critical answer always scores higher than a one-sided account. When asked to name greenhouse gases, specify all three: carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour. For pollutant questions, always state both the source and the specific harm caused — one mark each is typical.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The atmosphere evolved from a volcanic, \(CO_2\)-dominated early atmosphere through billions of years of photosynthesis, which added oxygen and removed carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide was also locked away in oceans, sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
  • The greenhouse effect is a natural warming process. Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb infrared radiation from Earth’s surface and re-emit it, warming the lower atmosphere. Human activities are enhancing this effect, causing global warming and climate change.
  • Burning fossil fuels also produces directly harmful pollutants: CO (toxic to blood), \(SO_2\) (acid rain), \(NO_x\) (acid rain and smog), and particulates (respiratory disease).

lessons.title: Earth's Resources: Water, Pollution and Sustainability
lessons.description: Potable water from fresh and salt sources, sewage treatment, sustainable development, and finite resources.
lessons.content_html:
Finite and Renewable Resources

The Earth provides natural resources that humans depend on for warmth, shelter, food and transport. Finite resources (also called non-renewable) will eventually be exhausted because they are consumed faster than they form. Examples include fossil fuels (which took millions of years to form) and metal ores mined from the Earth’s crust. Renewable resources can be replaced at roughly the same rate they are used — examples include timber from managed forests, crops, wind energy, solar energy and hydroelectric power.

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of today’s population without depleting resources that future generations will depend on. Chemistry plays a central role: designing industrial processes with higher atom economy, developing renewable and biodegradable materials, improving recycling technology, and creating more energy-efficient production routes all contribute to a more sustainable future.

Key Fact

Sustainable development: meeting current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It requires using finite resources wisely, recycling, reducing waste, and developing renewable alternatives.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not chemically pure — it still contains dissolved mineral salts — but has sufficiently low levels of dissolved substances and harmful microorganisms to be safe for human consumption. In the UK, most potable water is produced from fresh water sources such as rivers, lakes and reservoirs, through a multi-stage treatment process.

Step 1: Filtration — the water is passed through filter beds (layers of gravel and sand) to remove large solid particles and debris, including some suspended solids.

Step 2: Sterilisation — to kill harmful bacteria and microorganisms, the water is treated using chlorine, ozone, or ultraviolet (UV) light. Chlorine is the most commonly used method in the UK because it is effective, relatively cheap, and its residual effect continues to kill bacteria as the water travels through the distribution network to homes. Ozone and UV are used in some systems but provide no residual protection once the water leaves the treatment plant.

The treated water is then tested to ensure it meets drinking water standards before being distributed. The quality standards are set to protect public health.

Desalination

In countries with limited fresh water, potable water must be produced from sea water or brackish water. Desalination achieves this by removing dissolved salts. Two main methods are used:

Distillation: the sea water is heated until it boils, the water vapour is condensed and collected, leaving the dissolved salts behind. Reverse osmosis: sea water is forced under high pressure through a membrane that allows water molecules through but blocks dissolved salt ions. Both methods require large amounts of energy, making potable water produced by desalination considerably more expensive than that produced from fresh water. In the UK, where rainfall is generally sufficient, fresh water treatment is the primary approach. In arid regions, desalination is essential despite the high energy cost.

Key Fact

Desalination produces potable water from sea water by distillation (boiling and condensing) or reverse osmosis (high-pressure membrane filtration). Both methods require large amounts of energy, making desalinated water much more expensive than water treated from fresh sources.

Treating Waste Water

Waste water from homes, industry and agriculture must be treated before being returned to rivers or the sea, to prevent pollution and protect aquatic ecosystems. Sewage treatment is a multi-stage process involving both physical and biological methods.

1. Screening — large solid objects such as rags and sticks are removed by passing the sewage through coarse screens and grit channels. 2. Primary sedimentation — the screened sewage flows slowly through large settlement tanks. Heavier solids sink to form sludge, while lighter grease floats to the surface. Both are removed. 3. Biological treatment — the remaining liquid passes through aeration tanks where aerobic microorganisms break down dissolved organic matter. This biological stage is essential for removing dissolved organic pollutants. The sludge from sedimentation is also treated separately: anaerobic bacteria digest it, producing biogas (mainly methane) which can be used as a fuel. 4. Final clarification and sterilisation — the cleaned water undergoes further sedimentation, then is sterilised before being safely released into rivers.

Industrial waste water may contain heavy metals or toxic organic compounds and requires specialised treatment before release. Agricultural run-off containing nitrate fertilisers can cause eutrophication in waterways — excessive algal growth that depletes oxygen and harms aquatic life — if not properly managed.

Haber Process and NPK Fertilisers

Ammonia produced by the Haber process is a starting material not only for direct use as a fertiliser but for the production of NPK fertilisers — compound fertilisers containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in specific ratios. Nitrogen is provided by ammonium compounds or urea (both derived from ammonia), phosphorus from processed phosphate rock, and potassium from potash (potassium-containing minerals). These three elements are essential for healthy plant growth: nitrogen for leaf and stem growth, phosphorus for root development and energy transfer, and potassium for flower, fruit and disease resistance. The correct balance of N, P and K varies with soil type and crop, and is determined by soil analysis.

Key Fact

NPK fertilisers supply three key plant nutrients: nitrogen (N) for growth of leaves and stems, phosphorus (P) for root development and energy processes, and potassium (K) for flowers, fruits and disease resistance. Ammonia from the Haber process is the nitrogen source.

Sustainability in Resource Use

Sustainable management of Earth’s resources includes: reducing consumption of finite resources, recycling to recover valuable materials, developing biodegradable alternatives to persistent plastics, and improving industrial processes to reduce waste and pollution. The principle applies across every sector — from agriculture (sustainable fertiliser use to prevent eutrophication) to water management (reducing leakage and improving efficiency) to manufacturing (designing products for disassembly and recycling at end of life). Balancing economic development with environmental protection remains one of the central challenges of the 21st century.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on potable water, always distinguish between ‘potable’ and ‘pure’ — potable water is safe to drink but not chemically pure. A common error is to state that filtration alone makes water safe; you must also include sterilisation. For desalination questions, state the method (distillation or reverse osmosis) and explain why it is expensive (large energy input). For NPK questions, state what each letter stands for and the role of that element in plant growth — one mark per element is typical.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Potable water is safe to drink but not pure. In the UK it is produced from fresh water by filtration then sterilisation (usually with chlorine). Desalination (distillation or reverse osmosis) produces potable water from sea water but requires much more energy.
  • Sewage treatment uses screening, sedimentation and biological processes to remove solid and dissolved pollutants before water is returned to the environment. Industrial and agricultural run-off require additional specialist treatment.
  • Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising future generations. NPK fertilisers (from ammonia, phosphate rock and potash) supply the three essential plant nutrients nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

practice_questions.text: Explain why desalination is not widely used in the UK to produce potable water.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The UK has sufficient rainfall and fresh water sources (rivers, lakes, reservoirs) to meet demand; desalination requires large amounts of energy (for distillation or reverse osmosis), making it significantly more expensive than treating fresh water; the cost-benefit analysis does not favour desalination where fresh water is readily available.

practice_questions.text: Explain why agricultural run-off containing fertilisers can be harmful to rivers and lakes.

Emerging: States fertilisers pollute water with no mechanism described. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The only way to ensure everyone has access to safe drinking water is to build more desalination plants.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Desalination does expand access in water-scarce regions (coastal areas with limited fresh water); produces potable water from sea water regardless of rainfall; however it requires large energy inputs (expensive, often fossil fuel-powered, contributing to emissions); alternative approaches include improving fresh water treatment efficiency, reducing leakage in distribution systems, managing demand through pricing and education, and protecting catchment areas. A balanced conclusion reached — desalination is one solution among several, most appropriate where fresh water is genuinely scarce.
Secure: At least two advantages of desalination and two alternatives discussed; conclusion present.
Developing: Desalination described with one or two alternatives mentioned.
Emerging: General statement about water shortage with minimal analysis. [6 marks]
